source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5

coverage.syllabusReading: pp. 225–284 listed for first rulemaking range; uploaded text stops on p. 283
coverage.pending: Remainder of Chapter 5 from p. 284 and any later assigned rulemaking readings are not in this upload
coverage.status: New source-based chapter material only. Textbook problems and Notes & Questions remain unanswered.

topics.title: § 5.1 — Rise of Rulemaking & Agency Choice (pp. 225–233)
topics.description: Rulemaking versus adjudication; nine claimed advantages, five counterweights, ossification, scope of agency authority and ZIP-code-insurance problem.

entries.title: Rulemaking, adjudication, rules, orders
entries.summary: APA draws two processes: rulemaking develops a rule, while adjudication produces an order.
entries.laymanExplanation: APA draws two processes: rulemaking develops a rule, while adjudication produces an order.
entries.legalExplanation: §§ 551(4)–(7) distinguish prospective legal or policy statements from agency disposition of individual matters, though the boundary has difficult exceptions.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 225

entries.title: Why public participation favors rulemaking
entries.summary: All affected persons may participate through public comment and agencies must address significant comments, rather than confining formal participation to parties in individual hearings.
entries.laymanExplanation: All affected persons may participate through public comment and agencies must address significant comments, rather than confining formal participation to parties in individual hearings.
entries.legalExplanation: Rulemaking invites potentially affected people and organizations to contribute before a broad policy crystallizes. In adjudication, later parties may be affected by precedent without a chance to speak.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 225–226
entries.examApplication: In an exam, explain whether policy affects many people beyond named litigants and why public input is important.

entries.title: Why rulemaking is procedurally apt for legislative facts
entries.summary: Broad social, economic and scientific policy questions fit legislative-style submissions better than trial-style witness and credibility testing.
entries.laymanExplanation: Broad social, economic and scientific policy questions fit legislative-style submissions better than trial-style witness and credibility testing.
entries.legalExplanation: Rules concern general legislative facts, policy tradeoffs and expert data; adjudication's record/ex parte constraints may restrict policy information.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 226
entries.examApplication: Distinguish legislative facts from adjudicative facts; consider due process.

entries.title: Prospectivity and legitimate reliance
entries.summary: Rules normally operate prospectively and provide advance behavioral guidance, whereas new adjudicatory doctrines often apply to already completed conduct.
entries.laymanExplanation: Rules normally operate prospectively and provide advance behavioral guidance, whereas new adjudicatory doctrines often apply to already completed conduct.
entries.legalExplanation: A prospective standard reduces unfair surprise; an order that announces new policy may retroactively change outcome for an existing respondent.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 226
entries.examApplication: Compare § 5.2.2 Georgetown with § 4.5 retroactive adjudication.

entries.title: Uniformity across regulated class
entries.summary: A published rule regulates a defined class on shared terms, while individual case law immediately disposes of particular controversies.
entries.laymanExplanation: A published rule regulates a defined class on shared terms, while individual case law immediately disposes of particular controversies.
entries.legalExplanation: Rulemaking supplies general standards, avoiding arbitrary distinctions arising from unusual case facts.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 226
entries.examApplication: Identify class of regulated actors and whether a case-by-case approach would lead to inconsistent results.

entries.title: Political input and accountability
entries.summary: Rulemaking formalizes public policy participation and allows organized interests to advocate positions; trial-like adjudication is less suited to political tradeoffs.
entries.laymanExplanation: Rulemaking formalizes public policy participation and allows organized interests to advocate positions; trial-like adjudication is less suited to political tradeoffs.
entries.legalExplanation: Broad social-value decisions often deserve public debate rather than a fight confined to two named adversaries.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 226
entries.examApplication: Be clear that political input does not replace agency's statutory or reasoned decision obligations.

entries.title: Agency agenda control
entries.summary: Agency chooses which regulatory problem to prioritize and how to frame it, rather than waiting for an enforcement case with suitable facts.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency chooses which regulatory problem to prioritize and how to frame it, rather than waiting for an enforcement case with suitable facts.
entries.legalExplanation: One broad regulatory proceeding can target high-priority systemic problems; a particular case may be unsuitable as precedent.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 226–227
entries.examApplication: Relevant to ZIP-code pricing hypothetical.

entries.title: Policy efficiency in one general proceeding
entries.summary: A properly designed rule can resolve an issue for an industry in one proceeding rather than through repetitive litigation.
entries.laymanExplanation: A properly designed rule can resolve an issue for an industry in one proceeding rather than through repetitive litigation.
entries.legalExplanation: Rulemaking can involve heavy upfront costs but avoids dozens of duplicate adjudications.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 227
entries.examApplication: Discuss ossification counterargument.

entries.title: Publication and accessibility of rules
entries.summary: Published rules make obligations easier to locate than sometimes unpublished, unclear or inconsistent adjudicatory case law.
entries.laymanExplanation: Published rules make obligations easier to locate than sometimes unpublished, unclear or inconsistent adjudicatory case law.
entries.legalExplanation: Plain written standards can guide lawyers, firms and individuals before disputes arise.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 227
entries.examApplication: Contrast fact-specific dicta and inconsistent agency precedents.

entries.title: Executive and legislative oversight of rules
entries.summary: Rules are easier for the political branches to identify and review, with formal oversight schemes not ordinarily triggered by individual adjudicative decisions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Rules are easier for the political branches to identify and review, with formal oversight schemes not ordinarily triggered by individual adjudicative decisions.
entries.legalExplanation: A general published policy is easier to monitor and challenge than implicit policy produced through enforcement orders.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 227
entries.examApplication: Link to congressional and presidential rule review later in syllabus.

entries.title: Adjudication advantage: flexibility
entries.summary: Case-by-case development tailors law to concrete circumstances; general rules risk overbreadth, omissions or rigidity.
entries.laymanExplanation: Case-by-case development tailors law to concrete circumstances; general rules risk overbreadth, omissions or rigidity.
entries.legalExplanation: The regulator can observe how a principle works before deciding whether to generalize.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 227

entries.title: Adjudication advantage: emergent problems and limited expertise
entries.summary: Unexpected violations and novel fact patterns may require enforcement before an agency knows enough to design a wise prospective rule.
entries.laymanExplanation: Unexpected violations and novel fact patterns may require enforcement before an agency knows enough to design a wise prospective rule.
entries.legalExplanation: A rule not yet on the books cannot address every future problem; individual adjudication responds immediately.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 227–228

entries.title: Adjudication advantage: resource conservation
entries.summary: An agency may decide a narrower concrete case without expensive comprehensive studies and industrywide consultation.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency may decide a narrower concrete case without expensive comprehensive studies and industrywide consultation.
entries.legalExplanation: Use where a broad regulatory initiative would divert scarce resources.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 228

entries.title: Adjudication advantage: avoiding premature internal policy resolution
entries.summary: Individual cases can be decided without forcing policymakers to resolve all disputed general issues at once.
entries.laymanExplanation: Individual cases can be decided without forcing policymakers to resolve all disputed general issues at once.
entries.legalExplanation: Sometimes agency officials can agree on a specific outcome but not on a sweeping general formula.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 228

entries.title: Residual adjudication remains unavoidable
entries.summary: Even with extensive rules, ambiguous applications and exceptions will arise and require adjudication.
entries.laymanExplanation: Even with extensive rules, ambiguous applications and exceptions will arise and require adjudication.
entries.legalExplanation: Rules need interpretation in real-world cases.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 228

entries.title: Rulemaking ossification debate
entries.summary: 'Ossification' describes claims that judicial scrutiny, analytical obligations and procedural requirements slow or deter complex notice-and-comment rules.
entries.laymanExplanation: 'Ossification' describes claims that judicial scrutiny, analytical obligations and procedural requirements slow or deter complex notice-and-comment rules.
entries.legalExplanation: Some scholars say major technical rulemaking is overburdened; critics note agencies still promulgate many routine rules efficiently. The phenomenon's size and generality are disputed.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 228–229

entries.title: General enabling clauses and rules with force of law
entries.summary: A broad authorization to 'make rules and regulations' traditionally supports substantive legislative rules, but statutory text, context and limits still determine reach.
entries.laymanExplanation: A broad authorization to 'make rules and regulations' traditionally supports substantive legislative rules, but statutory text, context and limits still determine reach.
entries.legalExplanation: Do not assume an agency can legislate wherever it sees a beneficial policy; enabling law supplies power.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 230
entries.examApplication: Assess existence of delegated rulemaking power separately from legal scope of any particular regulation.

entries.title: National Petroleum Refiners Ass’n v. FTC, 482 F.2d 672 (D.C. Cir. 1973)
entries.summary: FTC's general § 6(g) rulemaking clause historically read to permit binding gas-station octane-posting standards despite prior reliance on adjudication.
entries.laymanExplanation: FTC's general § 6(g) rulemaking clause historically read to permit binding gas-station octane-posting standards despite prior reliance on adjudication.
entries.legalExplanation: Casebook notes later textualist skepticism of reading broad old clauses as substantive legislation.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 230
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Distinguish historical presumption from contemporary questions of delegated scope.

entries.title: Reasonably related to statute versus narrower express duties
entries.summary: Older Mourning approach generously upheld rules reasonably related to statutory purposes; later cases increasingly tether general clauses to specific powers and duties.
entries.laymanExplanation: Older Mourning approach generously upheld rules reasonably related to statutory purposes; later cases increasingly tether general clauses to specific powers and duties.
entries.legalExplanation: A general rulemaking sentence may not authorize programs beyond roles Congress assigned; major questions doctrine reinforces caution.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 230–231
entries.examApplication: Avoid claiming any general clause licenses a new private cause of action; compare text, specific functions, and context.

entries.title: Mourning v. Family Publications Service, 411 U.S. 356 (1973)
entries.summary: Traditional rule-scope test upheld rule when reasonably related to enabling legislation purposes.
entries.laymanExplanation: Traditional rule-scope test upheld rule when reasonably related to enabling legislation purposes.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook describes old generous interpretation of general delegations.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 230
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Contrast Chamber of Commerce and Florida.

entries.title: Chamber of Commerce v. NLRB, 721 F.3d 152 (4th Cir. 2013)
entries.summary: NLRB lacked power under general § 6 to require blanket employee-rights workplace posting outside its specifically assigned functions.
entries.laymanExplanation: NLRB lacked power under general § 6 to require blanket employee-rights workplace posting outside its specifically assigned functions.
entries.legalExplanation: Mourning presumption does not erase need to identify underlying delegated function.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 231
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Examine agency's specific statutory mission.

entries.title: Florida's statutory nondelegation § 120.536(1)
entries.summary: Florida expressly demands both rulemaking authorization and a specific law to implement; mere reasonable relation to legislative purposes is insufficient.
entries.laymanExplanation: Florida expressly demands both rulemaking authorization and a specific law to implement; mere reasonable relation to legislative purposes is insufficient.
entries.legalExplanation: The rule must implement or interpret concrete powers or duties, not just broad goals or policy.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 231–232
entries.examApplication: Separate general statutory authority from specific function; state case-law applications vary.

entries.title: St. Petersburg Kennel Club v. Department (Fla. 1998)
entries.summary: Florida cardroom regulator lacked specifically delegated authority to narrow poker definition to exclude Big Poker 21.
entries.laymanExplanation: Florida cardroom regulator lacked specifically delegated authority to narrow poker definition to exclude Big Poker 21.
entries.legalExplanation: Court invalidated rule even though casino statute generally allowed regulations.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 231–232
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Contrast later contextual decisions.

entries.title: Department v. Dania Entertainment Center (Fla. 2017)
entries.summary: Later Florida cardroom decision more willing to permit agency rules clarifying ambiguous assigned regulatory duties.
entries.laymanExplanation: Later Florida cardroom decision more willing to permit agency rules clarifying ambiguous assigned regulatory duties.
entries.legalExplanation: Shows later state law vacillation between rigid and functional delegation readings.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 232
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Do not overgeneralize one cardroom case.

topics.title: § 5.2.1 — What Is a Rule? (pp. 233–238)
topics.description: Federal APA versus 1961 MSAPA definitions; particular applicability and future effect; orders, ratemaking, policy guidance and unreviewable pronouncements.

entries.title: APA § 551(4): definition of rule
entries.summary: A rule is an agency statement of general or particular applicability and future effect that implements, interprets or prescribes law or policy or agency practice; definition expressly includes certain rate and corporate-reorganization matters.
entries.laymanExplanation: A rule is an agency statement of general or particular applicability and future effect that implements, interprets or prescribes law or policy or agency practice; definition expressly includes certain rate and corporate-reorganization matters.
entries.legalExplanation: Under federal law a forward-looking determination can count as rule even if it targets one utility; text alone is not always decisive.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 233

entries.title: APA § 551(6), (7): order and adjudication
entries.summary: An order is a final agency disposition other than rulemaking (including licensing); adjudication is the process of formulating an order.
entries.laymanExplanation: An order is a final agency disposition other than rulemaking (including licensing); adjudication is the process of formulating an order.
entries.legalExplanation: Definitions can be circular; inspect actual function of action rather than applying only literal labels.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 233–234

entries.title: Functional distinction: future policy versus concrete disposition
entries.summary: Rulemaking ordinarily determines prospective policies; adjudication ordinarily applies law to specific disputes, often concerning past conduct, but both categories have exceptions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Rulemaking ordinarily determines prospective policies; adjudication ordinarily applies law to specific disputes, often concerning past conduct, but both categories have exceptions.
entries.legalExplanation: Ask whether agency changes general obligations or resolves named parties' individual status based on a factual dispute.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 234–235
entries.examApplication: 'Particular applicability' and exclusively future effects do not automatically make every particular decision a rule.

entries.title: Neustar, Inc. v. FCC, 857 F.3d 886 (D.C. Cir. 2017)
entries.summary: FCC's bid award to Telcordia as number portability administrator was informal adjudication although particular in application and future in effect.
entries.laymanExplanation: FCC's bid award to Telcordia as number portability administrator was informal adjudication although particular in application and future in effect.
entries.legalExplanation: Selection resolved the specific case of competing bidders on individual facts, rather than prescribing policy.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 235
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Apply functional characterization despite literal § 551(4).

entries.title: Individual ratemaking and corporate reorganization exceptions
entries.summary: The federal APA expressly includes some particular future rates and corporate changes within rule definition; separate enabling statutes can nonetheless mandate formal hearing.
entries.laymanExplanation: The federal APA expressly includes some particular future rates and corporate changes within rule definition; separate enabling statutes can nonetheless mandate formal hearing.
entries.legalExplanation: A rate schedule for one named utility may be classed as rulemaking even though it affects one business.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 234–236
entries.examApplication: Check APA § 551(4) examples, whether enabling statute says on-the-record hearing, and due process requirements.

entries.title: 1961 MSAPA: general applicability only
entries.summary: Model state APA § 1(7) describes 'rule' as agency statement of general applicability, rather than the federal 'general or particular' formulation.
entries.laymanExplanation: Model state APA § 1(7) describes 'rule' as agency statement of general applicability, rather than the federal 'general or particular' formulation.
entries.legalExplanation: Do not mechanically transplant federal rule definition into state law.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 235–236
entries.examApplication: Explicitly compare state statutory wording and individual proceedings.

entries.title: Why classification changes procedure
entries.summary: Rulemaking often triggers § 553 notice and comment, while Type C adjudication provides fewer procedural rights; a claimant seeking trial-like due process may instead favor adjudication label.
entries.laymanExplanation: Rulemaking often triggers § 553 notice and comment, while Type C adjudication provides fewer procedural rights; a claimant seeking trial-like due process may instead favor adjudication label.
entries.legalExplanation: A procedural challenger may prefer different classifications depending on what protections are sought.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 236–237
entries.examApplication: Assess practical procedure before arguing one label is always better.

entries.title: Yesler Terrace Community Council v. Cisneros, 37 F.3d 442 (9th Cir. 1994)
entries.summary: HUD's prospective state-wide determination permitting housing authorities to avoid tenant grievance hearings was a rule, not a Type C case disposition.
entries.laymanExplanation: HUD's prospective state-wide determination permitting housing authorities to avoid tenant grievance hearings was a rule, not a Type C case disposition.
entries.legalExplanation: Decision affected broad unidentified population and no specific present dispute, demanding notice-and-comment procedure.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 236–237
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Use prospective class-wide impact as functional hallmark.

entries.title: Legislative rules and guidance can both fit APA rule definition
entries.summary: Binding legislative rules draw on delegated lawmaking authority; interpretive rules and policy statements lack force of law but may still be 'rules' for publication or review purposes.
entries.laymanExplanation: Binding legislative rules draw on delegated lawmaking authority; interpretive rules and policy statements lack force of law but may still be 'rules' for publication or review purposes.
entries.legalExplanation: Calling a document guidance does not necessarily take it outside the broad APA definition of rule.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 237
entries.examApplication: Distinguish definition of rule from whether notice/comment is required and whether action is final.

entries.title: Pronouncements lacking new legal or policy effect
entries.summary: A mere restatement or educational recommendation may not qualify as agency action subject to judicial review; courts examine legal impact, not title.
entries.laymanExplanation: A mere restatement or educational recommendation may not qualify as agency action subject to judicial review; courts examine legal impact, not title.
entries.legalExplanation: Government letter merely repeating old policy may leave legal situation unchanged; nonbinding health pamphlet may lack reviewable effect.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 237–238
entries.examApplication: Evaluate whether action implements/interprets/prescribes policy versus merely describes prevailing position.

entries.title: Independent Equipment Dealers Association v. EPA, 372 F.3d 420 (D.C. Cir. 2004)
entries.summary: EPA letter restating old engine-enforcement position not new reviewable agency action.
entries.laymanExplanation: EPA letter restating old engine-enforcement position not new reviewable agency action.
entries.legalExplanation: It 'left the world' unchanged under the source's functional analysis.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 237
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Check whether new binding position announced.

entries.title: Industrial Safety Equipment Association v. EPA, 837 F.2d 1115 (D.C. Cir. 1988)
entries.summary: NIOSH/EPA asbestos respirator guide recommended only two of thirteen approved respirators without legally decertifying the others.
entries.laymanExplanation: NIOSH/EPA asbestos respirator guide recommended only two of thirteen approved respirators without legally decertifying the others.
entries.legalExplanation: Court treated recommendation as educational publication not rule.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 237–238
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Look for lawfulness of all listed devices and practical versus legal effect.

topics.title: § 5.2.2 — Retroactivity & Bowen (pp. 239–246)
topics.description: True versus secondary retroactivity, express delegation, Bowen/Georgetown and Scalia concurrence; Landgraf and reliance examples.

entries.title: True (primary) retroactivity
entries.summary: New rule changes legal consequences of completed conduct or obligates repayment for a period already governed by prior law.
entries.laymanExplanation: New rule changes legal consequences of completed conduct or obligates repayment for a period already governed by prior law.
entries.legalExplanation: A rule enacted in 2026 cannot ordinarily penalize what was lawful in 2024 unless Congress gave special authority.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 239–243

entries.title: Secondary retroactivity
entries.summary: A prospective rule may reduce future value of earlier investments or contracts without retroactively rewriting legal consequences of acts completed in the past.
entries.laymanExplanation: A prospective rule may reduce future value of earlier investments or contracts without retroactively rewriting legal consequences of acts completed in the past.
entries.legalExplanation: You invested under old rules; new rules make your existing asset less profitable going forward.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 241–245

entries.title: Bowen v. Georgetown University Hospital, 488 U.S. 204 (1988)
entries.summary: No. General delegation to make rules does not authorize retroactive legislative rules without an express congressional grant; this Medicare scheme gave no such power.
entries.laymanExplanation: No. General delegation to make rules does not authorize retroactive legislative rules without an express congressional grant; this Medicare scheme gave no such power.
entries.legalExplanation: Did general Medicare rulemaking authority include power to issue a new binding cost-reimbursement rule retroactively recapturing past payments? Retroactivity is disfavored. Reissuing the formerly invalid rule with proper procedure could not erase the absence of statutory authorization to attach past financial consequences.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 239–240
entries.sourceRole: Case opinion reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: HHS's Medicare reimbursement formula was invalidated for lack of notice and comment; after readoption in 1984, HHS sought to recoup roughly $2 million from hospitals based on what it would have saved under rejected 1981 rule.
entries.issue: Did general Medicare rulemaking authority include power to issue a new binding cost-reimbursement rule retroactively recapturing past payments?
entries.holding: No. General delegation to make rules does not authorize retroactive legislative rules without an express congressional grant; this Medicare scheme gave no such power.
entries.reasoning: Retroactivity is disfavored. Reissuing the formerly invalid rule with proper procedure could not erase the absence of statutory authorization to attach past financial consequences.
entries.rule: Agency legislative rules generally cannot operate retroactively absent express statutory authorization; presumption disfavors retroactive reach.
entries.examApplication: First ask whether new legal consequences are attached to completed actions, then whether Congress authorized that kind of rule; distinguish case-by-case adjudication.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume curing defective notice-and-comment retroactively validates old repayment demands.

entries.title: Two Georgetown presumptions
entries.summary: Statutes and regulations ordinarily are not read retroactively unless language dictates it; delegation of legislative rulemaking ordinarily does not include authority to issue retroactive rules without express grant.
entries.laymanExplanation: Statutes and regulations ordinarily are not read retroactively unless language dictates it; delegation of legislative rulemaking ordinarily does not include authority to issue retroactive rules without express grant.
entries.legalExplanation: Ask both if text imposes past consequences and if agency has independent congressional power to do so.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 239–243
entries.examApplication: The Court distinguished rulemaking from retroactivity available through adjudication; separate textual presumptions from constitutional fairness.

entries.title: Scalia concurrence: 'future effect' in § 551(4)
entries.summary: Justice Scalia read the federal APA's rule definition as inherently prospective, though laws can prospectively affect earlier bargains; he framed alternative ground beyond majority's Medicare statutory holding.
entries.laymanExplanation: Justice Scalia read the federal APA's rule definition as inherently prospective, though laws can prospectively affect earlier bargains; he framed alternative ground beyond majority's Medicare statutory holding.
entries.legalExplanation: A rule can regulate what happens from now on even when it affects old investments.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 240–242
entries.examApplication: Concurrence is not majority holding; he criticized 'curative' retroactive rulemaking and preserved other agency authority such as adjudication.

entries.title: Landgraf v. USI Film Products, 511 U.S. 244 (1994)
entries.summary: Retroactivity requires judgment about whether new law attaches legal consequences to completed events, rather than merely touching facts predating enactment.
entries.laymanExplanation: Retroactivity requires judgment about whether new law attaches legal consequences to completed events, rather than merely touching facts predating enactment.
entries.legalExplanation: Procedural, jurisdictional and prospective relief statutes can sometimes apply to pending cases.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 243
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Use fair notice, reliance and settled expectations to identify true change.

entries.title: Interpretive rules and preexisting legal meaning
entries.summary: Guidance interpreting an already-existing statute may inform treatment of earlier events without necessarily creating a newly retroactive substantive requirement.
entries.laymanExplanation: Guidance interpreting an already-existing statute may inform treatment of earlier events without necessarily creating a newly retroactive substantive requirement.
entries.legalExplanation: Applying the meaning of old law is distinct from retroactively making new law.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 242–243
entries.examApplication: Textbook raises but does not settle complications involving interpretive rules and the 1961 MSAPA definition.
entries.examTrap: Do not automatically assume any interpretation of past conduct is forbidden rulemaking.

entries.title: National Cable & Telecommunications Association v. FCC, 567 F.3d 659 (D.C. Cir. 2009)
entries.summary: FCC could end exclusivity for future apartment cable services even though contracts already existed; rule altered future value of deals, not legality of past formation.
entries.laymanExplanation: FCC could end exclusivity for future apartment cable services even though contracts already existed; rule altered future value of deals, not legality of past formation.
entries.legalExplanation: Court upheld secondary retroactivity after weighing investment expectations and consumer competition benefits.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 244–245
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Apply reliance-versus-statutory-interest fairness.

entries.title: Arbitrary-and-capricious check for secondary retroactivity
entries.summary: An otherwise prospective rule may still be arbitrary if burdens on legitimate past reliance unreasonably outweigh regulatory benefits; not a categorical ban.
entries.laymanExplanation: An otherwise prospective rule may still be arbitrary if burdens on legitimate past reliance unreasonably outweigh regulatory benefits; not a categorical ban.
entries.legalExplanation: Even when the agency can act forward, it must reasonably confront severe disruptions to settled business investments.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 244–245
entries.examApplication: The balancing resembles manifest-injustice inquiry under retroactive adjudication, though Georgetown sets independent stricter rule for true legislative retroactivity.
entries.examTrap: Analyze foreseeability of change, magnitude of losses and continuing business opportunities.

problems.title: Ossification and procedural tradeoffs
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, p. 228–229
problems.prompt: Evaluate whether demanding notice, technical analysis and review improves participation or imposes unjustified burdens; do not decide.

problems.title: General versus specific agency rulemaking grant
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, p. 230–232
problems.prompt: Compare National Petroleum, Mourning, Chamber of Commerce and Florida-specific statutory limitation; identify how to approach source and scope of power.

problems.title: Madison Insurance Commission ZIP-code pricing problem
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, p. 232–233
problems.prompt: MIC can investigate auto insurance ZIP-code pricing via an individual complaint or consider general rulemaking; its statute grants broad power over unfair insurance practices. Compare approaches, costs, remedies, institutional experience, reliance and potential authority to invent a private damages action. Leave unanswered.

problems.title: Particular applicability in federal and state definitions
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, p. 235–236
problems.prompt: Contrast a future individualized rate or corporate reorganization with a bid adjudication; what hearing requirements may follow?

problems.title: Yesler, Neustar, and mere advice letters
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, p. 235–238
problems.prompt: Distinguish broad future class rights, individual factual award and nonbinding restatement; test APA classification consequences.

problems.title: Coal ash ABCE waiver petition and new closure conditions
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, p. 238
problems.prompt: EPA rejects ABCE's extension under existing Reg. 400 and also adds groundwater pumping and solidification requirements planned for all future operators. Distinguish Type C adjudication and possible new rule, then discuss rulemaking choice without deciding.

problems.title: Scalia's literal rule definition versus flexible practice
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, p. 242–243
problems.prompt: If a rule must have only future effect, is HHS retroactive pronouncement an order? Does the state APA's missing 'future effect' phrase alter the outcome?

problems.title: Combs disability guideline hypothetical
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, p. 243
problems.prompt: Applicant relied on obesity listing when applying in 1996, but SSA removed listing in 1999 before 2003 adjudication of 1996 benefits. Analyze which legal test should govern; do not resolve.

problems.title: Bernklau benefits assistance statute hypothetical
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, p. 244
problems.prompt: A new statute requiring Veterans Affairs assistance becomes effective during judicial review of denial; analyze pending-case consequences without answering.

problems.title: Figueroa training credit-hours hypothetical
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, p. 244
problems.prompt: Unemployment applicant relied on amended 'twelve credit hours or equivalent' rule while pending; agency applied earlier strict class-hours standard. Analyze possible retroactivity without solving.

problems.title: Colossal Coal Mining Directive 14–1 problem
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, p. 245–246
problems.prompt: State DNR announced but did not register a directive requiring rejection of permit applications whenever applicants have any unresolved prior environmental violation; used it against pending Colossal application. Classify whether this was a rule, publication duty, and possible retroactive application without answering.
